bank.q: In linguistics, a register refers to...
bank.a: A speaker's use of language in different circumstances, written or spoken
d: The list of words in a dictionary
The loudness of a person's voice
bank.why: Registers cover word choices, definitions, tone of voice, facial expressions and other verbal and non-verbal cues.

bank.q: Why do we show stylistic variation (registers)?
bank.a: We behave differently depending on who we are communicating with
d: Because grammar rules change every year
Because some words are hard to pronounce
bank.why: Since we behave differently according to who we communicate with, we present stylistic variation.

bank.q: Registers are influenced by which factors?
bank.a: Social occasion, purpose, participants (gender, age) and context
d: Only the topic of the conversation
bank.why: Social occasion, purpose, participants and context all shape the register.

bank.q: Which register is private and happens between close family members or intimate individuals?
bank.why: Intimate style is private: close family or intimate partners.

bank.q: Which register is common among peers and friends and uses jargon, slang, gay language or vulgar words?
bank.why: Casual style: peers and friends; slang, street language, gay language, even vulgar words.

bank.q: Which register is the "standard" one, requiring professional or mutually acceptable language?
bank.why: Consultative style is standard: teacher-student, employer-employee, doctor-patient, judge-lawyer, President and constituents.

bank.q: Which register is one-way, respectful, academic and legal, like sermons and the State of the Nation Address?
bank.why: Formal style is one-way: sermons, SONA, formal speeches, pronouncements by a judge.

bank.q: Which register is "frozen in time" and remains unchanged, mostly used in ceremonies?
bank.why: Frozen style never changes: the Preamble, the Lord's Prayer, the Pledge of Allegiance.

bank.q: What is the key difference between the consultative and the formal register?
bank.a: Formal is one-way; consultative involves exchange between the people talking
d: Formal uses slang; consultative does not
Consultative is used only in writing
Formal is private; consultative is public
bank.why: Unlike consultative, formal is one-way (a speech, a sermon, a pronouncement).

bank.q: Which is an example of the frozen register?
d: The State of the Nation Address
bank.why: Preamble, Lord's Prayer and the Allegiance are frozen. SONA is formal.

bank.term: The President delivers the State of the Nation A
bank.q: The President delivers the State of the Nation Address to Congress. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: A one-way, formal speech: formal register.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: The whole school recites the Panatang Makabayan
bank.q: The whole school recites the Panatang Makabayan at the flag ceremony. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: A fixed text recited the same way every time: frozen.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: A doctor explains a diagnosis and answers the pa
bank.q: A doctor explains a diagnosis and answers the patient's questions. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: Doctor and patient exchanging professional language: consultative.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: Two classmates chat in the canteen using slang a
bank.q: Two classmates chat in the canteen using slang and inside jokes. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: Peers using slang: casual.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: A married couple uses pet names and half-sentenc
bank.q: A married couple uses pet names and half-sentences only they understand. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: Private language between intimate partners: intimate.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: A judge reads the verdict aloud in a courtroom.
bank.q: A judge reads the verdict aloud in a courtroom. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: A judge's pronouncement is one-way and legal: formal. (A judge talking things over with a lawyer would be consultative.)
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: A lawyer and a judge discuss a motion during a h
bank.q: A lawyer and a judge discuss a motion during a hearing. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: Judge and lawyer exchanging professional language: consultative. (Reading the verdict alone would be formal.)
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: A priest gives the homily during Sunday Mass.
bank.q: A priest gives the homily during Sunday Mass. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: A sermon is one-way and respectful: formal.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: The congregation prays the Lord's Prayer togethe
bank.q: The congregation prays the Lord's Prayer together. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: The Lord's Prayer never changes: frozen.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: An employee asks the manager about the new sched
bank.q: An employee asks the manager about the new schedule during a meeting. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: Employer and employee using professional language: consultative.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: A student asks the teacher a question during con
bank.q: A student asks the teacher a question during consultation hours. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: Teacher and student, two-way and professional: consultative.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: A mother whispers goodnight to her child using a
bank.q: A mother whispers goodnight to her child using a special family nickname. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: Private language within close family: intimate.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: Teammates shout jokes and street language at eac
bank.q: Teammates shout jokes and street language at each other during practice. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: Peers with slang and street language: casual.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.term: A valedictorian delivers a prepared speech at gr
bank.q: A valedictorian delivers a prepared speech at graduation. Which register is BEST shown?
bank.why: A prepared one-way speech at a ceremony: formal. It is not frozen because the words are new each time.
bank.hint: Who is talking, and is it one-way or two-way?

bank.q: Being competent in grammar, structure, phonology, morphology, semantics and the 5 macro skills is...
bank.why: Linguistic competence = the language system itself.

bank.q: Using appropriate words, expressions, attitude and body language for a specific topic, setting and group is...
bank.why: Sociolinguistic = language in society: what is appropriate for a setting and community.

bank.q: Being able to clarify and find solutions to communication ambiguities and confusion is...
bank.why: Strategic = repairing communication when it breaks down.

bank.q: Initiating, developing, turn-taking, shifting, repairing and ending conversations is...
bank.why: Discourse = managing a conversation from start to finish.

bank.q: A tourist looks confused, so you say the directions again with simpler words and point on a map. Which competence are you showing?
bank.why: Clearing up confusion and finding another way to get the message across is strategic competence.

bank.q: In a group discussion, you wait for a pause, add your point, then invite a quiet member to speak. Which competence is this?
bank.why: Turn-taking and moving the conversation along are discourse competence.

bank.q: You switch to "po" and "opo" and a respectful tone when talking to your friend's grandparents. Which competence?
bank.why: Choosing words and attitude appropriate to the people and setting is sociolinguistic.

bank.q: You correct your subject-verb agreement before submitting an essay. Which competence?
bank.why: Grammar and structure belong to linguistic competence.

bank.q: According to the slides, how do registers relate to the communicative competencies?
bank.a: Any register can be part of any of the competencies
d: Only the formal register uses competencies
Each register matches exactly one competence
bank.why: All registers of speech can be part of any of the communicative competencies.

bank.q: The British spelling is "colour". What is the American spelling?
bank.why: British colour → American color. Patterns: -our/-or, -re/-er, -ise/-ize, -ll-/-l-, -mme/-m.

bank.q: The British spelling is "centre". What is the American spelling?
bank.why: British centre → American center. Patterns: -our/-or, -re/-er, -ise/-ize, -ll-/-l-, -mme/-m.

bank.q: The British spelling is "realise". What is the American spelling?
bank.why: British realise → American realize. Patterns: -our/-or, -re/-er, -ise/-ize, -ll-/-l-, -mme/-m.

bank.q: The British spelling is "traveller". What is the American spelling?
bank.why: British traveller → American traveler. Patterns: -our/-or, -re/-er, -ise/-ize, -ll-/-l-, -mme/-m.

bank.q: The British spelling is "programme". What is the American spelling?
bank.why: British programme → American program. Patterns: -our/-or, -re/-er, -ise/-ize, -ll-/-l-, -mme/-m.

bank.q: "Football" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British football = American soccer.

bank.q: "Autumn" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British autumn = American fall.

bank.q: "Flat" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British flat = American apartment.

bank.q: "Biscuit" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British biscuit = American cookie.

bank.q: "Trousers" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British trousers = American pants.

bank.q: "Petrol" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British petrol = American gasoline.

bank.q: "Lorry" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British lorry = American truck.

bank.q: "Queue" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British queue = American line.

bank.q: "Torch" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British torch = American flashlight.

bank.q: "Rubber" in British English is called what in American English?
bank.why: British rubber = American eraser.

bank.q: The Filipinism "Xerox (this)" is better said as...
bank.why: Filipinism: Xerox (this) → better: Photocopy (this)
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.q: The Filipinism "Sewer (for a dressmaker)" is better said as...
bank.why: Filipinism: Sewer (for a dressmaker) → better: Tailor / seamstress
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.q: The Filipinism "There's traffic." is better said as...
bank.why: Filipinism: There's traffic. → better: There's heavy traffic.
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.q: The Filipinism "Bottomless (drinks)" is better said as...
bank.why: Filipinism: Bottomless (drinks) → better: Refillable
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.q: The Filipinism "Come again?" is better said as...
bank.a: Could you say that again, please?
bank.why: Filipinism: Come again? → better: Could you say that again, please?
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.q: The Filipinism "Fill up (a form)" is better said as...
bank.why: Filipinism: Fill up (a form) → better: Fill out / fill in
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.term: Filipinism: Pass by my office later.
bank.q: The Filipinism "Pass by my office later." is better said as...
bank.why: Filipinism: Pass by my office later. → better: Drop by my office later.
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.q: The Filipinism "Fall in line." is better said as...
bank.a: Get in line / make a line.
bank.why: Filipinism: Fall in line. → better: Get in line / make a line.
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.q: The Filipinism "For a while." is better said as...
bank.a: Just a second / just a moment.
bank.why: Filipinism: For a while. → better: Just a second / just a moment.
bank.hint: How would a native speaker say it?

bank.q: What is a Filipinism?
bank.a: An expression used by Filipino speakers that differs from standard English usage
d: A Tagalog word with no English meaning
A British spelling used in the Philippines
A formal register used in government
bank.why: Filipinisms are English expressions shaped by Filipino usage, like "fill up a form" for fill out.

bank.q: Gender-neutral language is a generic term covering which kinds of language?
d: Politically correct and euphemistic language only
bank.why: European Parliament (2018): gender-neutral language covers non-sexist, inclusive or gender-fair language.

bank.q: What is the main purpose of gender-neutral language?
bank.a: To avoid word choices that imply one sex or social gender is the norm
d: To replace all pronouns with names
bank.why: It avoids word choices that may be biased, discriminatory or demeaning by implying one sex is the norm.

bank.q: Besides avoiding bias, gender-fair language also helps to...
bank.a: Reduce stereotyping, promote social change and achieve gender equality
bank.why: It reduces gender stereotyping, promotes social change and contributes to gender equality.

bank.q: Which pronouns do the slides offer for gender-neutral reference?
bank.why: They/them/their avoid assuming a person's gender.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "chairman"?
bank.why: chairman → Chair, chairperson or coordinator. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "forefathers"?
bank.why: forefathers → Ancestors or forebears. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "man-made"?
bank.why: man-made → Artificial or manufactured. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "common man"?
bank.why: common man → Average or ordinary person. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "freshman"?
bank.why: freshman → First-year student. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "stewardess"?
bank.why: stewardess → Flight attendant. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "congressman"?
bank.why: congressman → Legislator or representative. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "mailman / postman"?
bank.why: mailman / postman → Mail carrier or postal worker. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "policeman"?
bank.why: policeman → Police officer. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "brotherhood"?
bank.why: brotherhood → Solidarity. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "to man (a booth)"?
bank.why: to man (a booth) → To operate, to cover, to staff. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: What is the gender-neutral replacement for "man (as in all people)"?
bank.why: man (as in all people) → People, person or individual. Words like chairwoman or postwoman just swap the gender; they are not neutral.
bank.hint: Remove the gender, don't swap it.

bank.q: "Solidarity" is the gender-neutral replacement for which word?
bank.why: Solidarity replaces brotherhood.
bank.hint: Which old word had "man" or "-ess" in it?

bank.q: "Flight attendant" is the gender-neutral replacement for which word?
bank.why: Flight attendant replaces stewardess.
bank.hint: Which old word had "man" or "-ess" in it?

bank.q: "First-year student" is the gender-neutral replacement for which word?
bank.why: First-year student replaces freshman.
bank.hint: Which old word had "man" or "-ess" in it?

bank.q: "Legislator" is the gender-neutral replacement for which word?
bank.why: Legislator replaces congressman.
bank.hint: Which old word had "man" or "-ess" in it?

bank.q: Politically correct terms are...
bank.a: Terms meant to give the least offense when describing groups identified by markers like race, gender, culture or orientation
d: Formal words used in legal documents
bank.why: PC language aims to give the least offense; it is rooted in a desire to eliminate exclusion of identity groups (Britannica, 2024).

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "cheating"?
bank.why: "Cheating" → academic dishonesty.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.q: "Aesthetically challenged" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Aesthetically challenged replaces "ugly".

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "disabled"?
bank.why: "Disabled" → differently-abled.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.q: "Drug dependent" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Drug dependent replaces "drug addict".

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "broken home"?
bank.why: "Broken home" → dysfunctional family.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.q: "Economically marginalized" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Economically marginalized replaces "poor".

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "old"?
bank.why: "Old" → elderly / senior.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.q: "Hearing impaired" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Hearing impaired replaces "deaf".

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "squatters"?
bank.why: "Squatters" → informal settlers.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.q: "Intellectual disability" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Intellectual disability replaces "mental retardation".

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "short"?
bank.why: "Short" → vertically challenged.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.q: "Nondiscretionary fragrance" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Nondiscretionary fragrance replaces "body odor".

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "homeless"?
bank.why: "Homeless" → outdoor urban.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.term: PC: horizontally challenged / people of mass
bank.q: "Horizontally challenged / people of mass" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Horizontally challenged / people of mass replaces "fat".

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "rape victim"?
bank.why: "Rape victim" → rape survivor.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.q: "Visually challenged" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Visually challenged replaces "blind".

bank.q: What is the politically correct term for "computer illiterate"?
bank.why: "Computer illiterate" → technologically challenged.
bank.hint: Pick the gentlest, least offensive term.

bank.q: "Socially misaligned" is the politically correct term for...
bank.why: Socially misaligned replaces "psychopath".

bank.q: You are writing a memo to every employee in the office. Which greeting is BEST?
bank.why: "Dear colleagues" includes everyone without naming a gender. "Dear Sir/Madam" is fairer than "Sirs" but still sorts people by gender.

bank.q: Choose the BEST pronoun: "Each student should bring ___ own laptop."
bank.why: The slides give they/them/their for gender-neutral reference.

bank.q: A shop posts: "Wanted: a reliable salesman." Which revision is BEST?
d: Wanted: a reliable salesman or saleslady.
bank.why: Swap -man for -person instead of swapping the gender.

bank.q: The committee is headed by Ms. Cruz. How should the host introduce her role, following gender-neutral language?
bank.why: Chairperson (or chair) is neutral. Chairwoman and chairlady still mark gender; Madam Chairman keeps "man".

bank.q: A brochure says "Man has always dreamed of exploring space." Which revision is BEST?
bank.a: People have always dreamed of exploring space.
d: Men have always dreamed of exploring space.
Man and woman have always dreamed of exploring space.
Mankind has always dreamed of exploring space.
bank.why: "Man" for all people → people, person or individual. Mankind keeps the same bias.

bank.q: A sign reads "The help desk will be manned by volunteers." Which revision is BEST?
bank.a: The help desk will be staffed by volunteers.
d: The help desk will be womanned by volunteers.
The help desk will be guarded by volunteers.
The help desk will be mastered by volunteers.
bank.why: "To man" → to operate, to cover, to staff.

bank.q: A speech says "Our forefathers built this town." Which wording is BEST?
d: Our forefathers and foremothers built this town.
Our old men built this town.
bank.why: Forefathers → ancestors or forebears.

bank.q: A news report describes families living along the riverbank without land titles. Which term is BEST?
bank.why: "Squatters" → informal settlers. Outdoor urban is the PC term for homeless, which is a different situation.
bank.hint: They have homes, just no land titles.

bank.q: A barangay announces a program for residents who use wheelchairs. Which term is BEST?
bank.why: Disabled → differently-abled.

bank.q: A teacher writes a formal report about a student caught copying answers. Which term is BEST?
bank.why: Cheating → academic dishonesty. Ethnically disoriented is the slides' (odd) PC term for dishonest in general, not for cheating in school.

bank.q: A news story covers a woman who lived through a sexual assault and is now speaking out. Which term is BEST?
bank.why: Rape victim → rape survivor.

bank.q: A hospital form asks about a patient who cannot hear. Which term is BEST?
bank.why: Deaf → hearing impaired. Visually challenged is for blind.

bank.q: A city scholarship targets students from low-income families. Which description is BEST?
bank.why: Poor → economically marginalized. Informal settlers refers to housing, not income.

bank.q: A barangay plans a day for residents aged 65 and above. Which term is BEST?
bank.why: Old → elderly or senior.

bank.q: A rehabilitation center describes the people in its program. Which term is BEST?
bank.why: Drug addict → drug dependent.

bank.q: An office memo refers to employees who need training on computers. Which term is BEST?
bank.why: Computer illiterate → technologically challenged.

bank.q: Phonetics is the scientific study of what?
bank.why: Phonetics is the scientific study of sounds: phones and phonemes.

bank.q: Which of these are the segmental features of speech?
bank.why: Segmentals are the individual sounds: consonants, vowels and diphthongs.

bank.q: Suprasegmentals are also called what?
bank.why: Phonetics includes the segmentals and the suprasegmentals (prosody or prosodic features) such as stress, pitch and intonation.

bank.q: "To", "too" and "two" show which spelling problem in English?
bank.a: Different letters can represent the same sound
d: The same letter can represent different sounds
A combination of letters can represent one sound
bank.why: All three are pronounced [tu] but are spelled differently.

bank.term: Letter a in cake, mat, call
bank.q: The letter a in cake, mat, call, any and sofa is pronounced five different ways. This shows that...
bank.a: The same letter can represent different sounds
d: Different letters can represent the same sound
A combination of letters can represent one sound
bank.why: One letter, a, stands for five different vowel sounds.

bank.q: The gh in rough, the ph in physics and the ea in head each stand for a single sound. This shows that...
bank.a: A combination of letters can represent one sound
d: Different letters can represent the same sound
The same letter can represent different sounds
bank.why: Two letters are written, but only one sound is pronounced.

bank.q: Bomb, knee, debt and receipt are examples of which spelling problem?
d: Different letters for the same sound
A combination of letters for one sound
bank.why: These words contain silent letters: the b in bomb and debt, the k in knee, the p in receipt.
bank.hint: Some letters are not pronounced at all.

bank.q: When the letter c comes before i, e or y (city, cent, cyst), it is pronounced as...
bank.why: c before i, e and y = /s/: city, cigar, certain, cent, cyst.

bank.q: When the letter c comes before a, o or u, or ends a word (cat, cup, plastic), it is pronounced as...
bank.why: c before a, o, u and at the end of a word = /k/: cat, cone, cup, plastic.

bank.q: Following the slides' rule for the letter c, how are the two c's in "circus" pronounced?
bank.why: The first c comes before i, so it is /s/; the second comes before u, so it is /k/.
bank.hint: Look at the vowel after each c.

bank.q: "Electric" and "electricity" keep the same spelling even though the c changes from /k/ to /s/. What does this show?
bank.a: English spelling keeps related words alike even when pronunciation changes
d: The letter c is always silent in long words
bank.why: Related words keep the same spelling even though the pronunciation of c changes.

bank.q: In philosophy, physics and photograph, the letter combination p + h is pronounced as...
bank.why: p alone is /p/ (put, top), but p + h = /f/.

bank.q: Using English spelling, "ghoti" can be read as which word?
bank.why: gh as in rough (/f/), o as in women (/ɪ/), ti as in nation (/š/): f-i-sh.

bank.q: In "ghoti" (fish), the ti is pronounced like the ti in which word?
bank.why: The ti in nation is pronounced /š/, giving the sh at the end of fish.

bank.q: Per the slides, the letter s in "resign" is pronounced as...
bank.why: The letter s has 3 sounds: see [s], pleasure [š / ž], resign [z].

bank.q: "Place of articulation" refers to what?
bank.a: Where in the mouth the airstream is obstructed
d: How long a sound is held
bank.why: Place = where the airstream is obstructed; manner = how; voicing = vocal cord vibration.

bank.q: English consonants are described by which three things?
bank.a: Place of articulation, manner of articulation and voicing
d: Tongue height, advancement and lip rounding
bank.why: Consonants: place (where), manner (how) and voicing (vocal cords). The other sets describe vowels or suprasegmentals.

bank.q: Which set of sounds is bilabial?
bank.why: Bilabial = both lips: /p/, /b/, /m/ and /w/.

bank.q: Labiodental sounds are made with which articulators?
d: Back of the tongue and the soft palate
bank.why: The top teeth touch the bottom lip: /f/ and /v/.

bank.q: Which sounds are interdental?
bank.why: Interdental: the tongue tip is between the teeth, as in think /θ/ and this /ð/.

bank.q: According to the slides, which sounds are especially difficult for second-language learners because few languages have them?
bank.why: θ and ð are not common sounds in many of the world's languages.

bank.q: Which set is made at the alveolar (tooth) ridge?
bank.why: Alveolar: the tongue tip touches the ridge just behind the upper teeth.
bank.hint: The biggest group on the chart.

bank.q: Palatal (alveo-palatal or post-alveolar) sounds are made with which part of the tongue?
bank.a: The blade, approaching the hard palate
d: The back, touching the soft palate
The tip, touching the tooth ridge
bank.why: The blade of the tongue approaches the hard palate just behind the tooth ridge: /š/, /ž/, /č/, /ǰ/, /y/.

bank.q: The sound /ž/ (/ʒ/) rarely begins an English word. Which word, from the slides, does begin with it?
bank.why: /ž/ rarely starts English words; foreign-origin words like genre and Jacques do. Measure, beige and vision have it in the middle or at the end.

bank.q: Velar sounds are made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate. Which are they?
bank.why: Velar (velum = soft palate): /k/, /g/ and /ŋ/ (ng).

bank.q: What is the glottis?
bank.a: The space between the vocal folds
d: The ridge behind the upper teeth
bank.why: English has two glottal sounds: /h/ and the glottal stop /ʔ/.

bank.q: When you say "uh-oh", there is a catch before each vowel. Which sound is it, and where is it made?
bank.a: The glottal stop /ʔ/, at the glottis
bank.why: The glottal stop in uh-oh occurs before each vowel sound; it is made at the glottis.

bank.q: A speaker places the tongue tip between the teeth to begin the word "think". What place of articulation is this?
bank.why: Tongue between (inter) the teeth (dental): /θ/.

bank.q: On the slides' chart, where is /w/ placed?
bank.why: /w/ is listed with the bilabials /p/, /b/, /m/ (lips rounded).

bank.q: On the slides' chart, where is /y/ placed?
bank.why: /y/ is a palatal glide: the blade of the tongue approaches the hard palate.
bank.hint: Same column as š and č.

bank.q: "Manner of articulation" refers to what?
bank.why: Manner = the way the obstruction is achieved: stops, fricatives, affricates, nasals, liquids, glides.

bank.q: Consonants made with a complete blockage of the airstream are called...
bank.why: Stops/plosives: /p/, /b/, /t/, /d/, /k/, /g/.

bank.q: Which sounds are made with partial obstruction that causes friction in the airflow?
bank.why: Fricatives (continuants): /f/, /v/, /s/, /z/, /θ/, /ð/, /š/, /ž/.

bank.q: An affricate is a combination of which two manners?
bank.a: A stop followed immediately by a fricative
d: A fricative followed by a nasal
A nasal followed by a glide
A glide followed by a stop
bank.why: Chug begins as /t/ and is released as a fricative; jug begins as /d/. Affricates: /č/, /ǰ/.

bank.q: How are nasal sounds produced?
bank.a: The soft palate is lowered so air escapes through the nose
d: The lips round while the tongue nears the soft palate
Air passes over the sides of the tongue
bank.why: Nasals/sonorants: /m/, /n/, /ŋ/; air is blocked in the mouth and escapes through the nose.
bank.hint: Pinch your nose and try to say m.

bank.q: Which sounds are the liquids or approximants?
bank.why: Liquids/approximants: the lateral /l/ and the retroflex /r/; air passes through the mouth in a fluid manner.

bank.q: Why is /l/ called a lateral liquid?
bank.a: Air passes over the sides of the tongue
bank.why: For /l/, the tongue tip touches the tooth ridge and air flows over the sides (laterals) of the tongue.

bank.q: Why is /r/ called a retroflex liquid?
bank.a: The tongue tip is slightly curled back
d: Air passes over the sides of the tongue
bank.why: Retroflex = bent back: the tongue tip curls slightly back for /r/.

bank.q: Which sounds are the glides or semi-vowels?
bank.why: Glides (semi-vowels) are made with a relatively wide opening, like vowels.

bank.q: Fricatives with hissing sounds, like /s/, /z/, /š/ and /ž/, are called...
bank.why: Hissing fricatives are sibilants.

bank.q: Stops, fricatives and affricates, where air is not let out through the nose, are together called...
bank.why: Consonants made without air through the nose are obstruents.

bank.q: A voiced sound is one made...
d: With no vibration of the vocal cords
With air escaping through the nose
bank.why: Voiced (+): vocal cords vibrate. Voiceless (-): no vibration.
bank.hint: Feel the buzz in your throat.

bank.q: The vocal cords are bands of muscle attached to the walls of the...
bank.why: The vocal cords are in the larynx; held close together they vibrate, held apart they do not.

bank.q: Which pair differs ONLY in voicing?
bank.why: /s/ and /z/ are both alveolar fricatives; /s/ is voiceless and /z/ is voiced.

bank.q: Which of these is NOT a fricative?
bank.why: /č/ is an affricate (stop + fricative), not a fricative.
bank.hint: One of them begins with a stop.

bank.q: Put your hand on your throat and say "zzz" and then "sss". You feel buzzing only for "zzz". What feature does this show?
bank.why: /z/ is voiced (vocal cords vibrate) and /s/ is voiceless; everything else about them is the same.

bank.q: With your nose pinched, "mama" and "no" sound blocked, but "papa" and "toe" sound normal. Which manner of articulation is affected?
bank.why: /m/ and /n/ are nasals: their air escapes through the nose.

bank.q: What mainly separates vowels from consonants?
bank.a: Vowels have a wide opening and little obstruction of the airstream
d: Vowels are made only at the lips
bank.why: Vowels are made with a wide opening, so there is little obstruction compared with consonants.

bank.q: Which are the four characteristics used to describe vowels?
bank.a: Tongue height, tongue advancement, tenseness/laxness, lip rounding
bank.why: Vowels: tongue height (high/mid/low), advancement (front/central/back), tense/lax and rounded/unrounded.
bank.hint: All about the tongue and lips.

bank.q: Vowels vary greatly by dialect. Which factors does the variation depend on?
bank.a: Region, social class, education, age and gender
d: Only the spelling of the word
bank.why: Vowel variation depends on geographical region, social class, educational background, age and gender.

bank.q: The vowel in "beat" (/i/) is described as...
bank.why: /i/: beat, east, leap = high front tense unrounded.

bank.q: The vowel in "bit" (/ɪ/) is described as...
bank.why: /ɪ/: bit, if, big = high front lax unrounded.

bank.q: The vowel in "bat" (/æ/) is described as...
bank.why: /æ/: bat, laugh, cat, and = low front lax unrounded.

bank.q: The vowel in "boot" (/u/) is described as...
bank.why: /u/: boot, who, duty = high back tense rounded.

bank.q: The vowel in "book" (/ʊ/) is described as...
bank.why: /ʊ/: book, put, foot, could = high back lax rounded.

bank.q: The vowel in "bought" (/ɔ/) is described as...
bank.why: /ɔ/: bought, caught, ball, law = mid back lax rounded.

bank.q: Which vowel is the first sound of "among" and "ago" and the last sound of "sofa"?
bank.why: /ə/ (schwa): among, sofa, ago = mid central unrounded.

bank.q: On the slides' vowel chart, which vowels are rounded?
bank.why: Only the back vowels u, ʊ, o, ɔ are rounded; /a/ is the unrounded low back vowel.

bank.q: Tense vowels differ from lax vowels because they are...
bank.a: Produced with extra muscle tension and the tongue slightly higher
d: Produced with no tension at all
bank.why: Tense vowels have extra muscle tension, sometimes spread lips, and a slightly higher tongue than their lax counterparts.

bank.q: Diphthongs are...
d: Silent vowels at the end of a word
bank.why: Diphthongs are complex vowels: /aɪ/ (bite), /aʊ/ (bout), /ɔɪ/ (boy).

bank.q: Boy, coin, voice and oyster share which diphthong?
bank.why: /ɔɪ/: boy, doily, rejoice, annoy, oil, voice, oyster, coin.

bank.q: House, brown, loud and now share which diphthong?
bank.why: /aʊ/: bout, brown, doubt, flower, ounce, house, now, loud.

bank.q: Eye, sky, tie and island share which diphthong?
bank.why: /aɪ/: bite, aisle, choir, island, eye, dry, by, tie, sky, hide.

bank.q: Rhoticization refers to vowels that are...
bank.a: r-colored, like the vowel in bird and work
d: Nasalized, like the vowel in French bon
Rounded, like the vowel in boot
bank.why: Rhoticization (r-coloring): a vowel plus /r/ quality, written /ɝ/ or /ɚ/: earn, work, bird, player.

bank.q: Which word has a lax vowel?
bank.why: bit has /ɪ/ (lax); beat /i/, boot /u/ and bait /e/ are tense.

bank.q: Your teacher writes: /ən/ is used instead of /ə/ before "apple", "hour", "honest" and "umbrella". What kind of sound begins all of these words?
bank.why: "An" goes before a vowel SOUND. The h in hour and honest is silent, so those words begin with a vowel sound too.
bank.hint: Hour and honest: is the h pronounced?

bank.q: Which word is preceded by "an" (/ən/)?
bank.why: Hour begins with a vowel sound (silent h). University begins with the glide /y/, one with /w/, and house with /h/.
bank.hint: Listen to the first sound, not the first letter.

bank.q: In one accent, speakers skip the l in "walk", "talk", "calm" and "half", and the r in "car", "park" and "hard" after the vowel, but pronounce every other consonant. What segmental feature do the skipped sounds share?
bank.why: The only sounds affected are /l/ and /r/, and those two are the liquids (approximants): lateral /l/ and retroflex /r/.
bank.hint: Which two sounds keep getting skipped?

bank.q: The plural -s sounds like /s/ in "cats", "cups" and "books" but like /z/ in "dogs", "bags" and "pens". Which feature of the final sound decides this?
bank.why: After voiceless /t/, /p/, /k/ the ending is voiceless /s/; after voiced /g/, /n/ it is voiced /z/.
bank.hint: Buzz or no buzz in the last sound.

bank.q: The -ed in "walked" sounds like /t/ but in "played" like /d/. What decides it?
bank.a: Whether the sound before it is voiced or voiceless
d: The place of articulation of the vowel
bank.why: /k/ in walk is voiceless, so -ed is /t/; the vowel in play is voiced, so -ed is /d/. /t/ and /d/ differ only in voicing.

bank.q: The prefix in- becomes im- before possible, balance and mature (impossible, imbalance, immature). The /m/ matches the next sound in which feature?
bank.why: /p/, /b/ and /m/ are all bilabial, so /n/ changes to the bilabial nasal /m/.
bank.hint: p, b, m are made with the same body part.

bank.q: A child says "fink" for "think", replacing /θ/ with /f/. What do the two sounds have in common?
bank.why: /θ/ is an interdental fricative and /f/ a labiodental fricative; both are voiceless. Only the place changes.

bank.q: A speaker says "pish" for "fish", replacing /f/ with /p/. What do /f/ and /p/ share?
bank.why: /f/ is a labiodental fricative and /p/ a bilabial stop, so place and manner both change; they share voicing (both red on the chart).

bank.q: A speaker says "bery" for "very", replacing /v/ with /b/. What do /v/ and /b/ share?
bank.why: /v/ is a voiced labiodental fricative and /b/ a voiced bilabial stop. They share voicing (and both use the lips).

bank.q: The first sounds of "snake", "zoo" and "shoe" and the middle sound of "measure" form which group?
bank.why: /s/, /z/, /š/, /ž/ are hissing fricatives: sibilants.

bank.q: The "ng" at the end of "sing" is a single sound. Which one?
bank.why: ng is one sound, /ŋ/: velar (back of tongue) and nasal.
bank.hint: Back of the tongue, through the nose.

bank.q: Which word ENDS with an affricate?
bank.why: judge ends with /ǰ/ (affricate). jazz ends with /z/ (fricative), hush with /š/ (fricative), bang with /ŋ/ (nasal).

bank.q: In "pat" and "cat", the air is stopped completely and then released in a small burst. Which manner?
bank.why: /p/, /t/, /k/ involve complete blockage, then release: stops or plosives.

bank.q: The first sounds of "yes" and "wet" are made with a wide opening, almost like vowels. What are they called?
bank.why: /y/ and /w/ are glides or semi-vowels.

bank.q: A learner pronounces "vine" as "fine". Which feature of the first sound changed?
bank.why: /v/ and /f/ are both labiodental fricatives; /v/ is voiced, /f/ voiceless.

Intimate — private, close family or partners | Casual — peers, slang, jargon | Consultative — standard, two-way, professional (teacher-student, doctor-patient, judge-lawyer) | Formal — one-way, respectful (SONA, sermon, verdict) | Frozen — never changes (Preamble, Lord's Prayer, Pledge)
Competencies

Linguistic — grammar, phonology, 5 macro skills | Sociolinguistic — appropriate words and body language for the setting | Strategic — clarifying, fixing confusion | Discourse — starting, turn-taking, ending conversations
British vs American

colour — color | centre — center | realise — realize | traveller — traveler | programme — program | football — soccer | autumn — fall | flat — apartment | biscuit — cookie | petrol — gasoline | lorry — truck | queue — line
Filipinisms

xerox — photocopy | sewer — tailor, seamstress | there's traffic — heavy traffic | bottomless — refillable | come again? — could you say that again? | fill up — fill out | pass by — drop by | fall in line — get in line | for a while — just a moment
Gender-neutral

chairman — chairperson, chair | forefathers — ancestors | man-made — artificial | common man — ordinary person | freshman — first-year student | stewardess — flight attendant | congressman — legislator | mailman — mail carrier | policeman — police officer | brotherhood — solidarity | to man — to staff | man — people, person | Pronouns — they, them, their
Politically correct

cheating — academic dishonesty | disabled — differently-abled | drug addict — drug dependent | broken home — dysfunctional family | poor — economically marginalized | old — elderly, senior | deaf — hearing impaired | squatters — informal settlers | homeless — outdoor urban | blind — visually challenged | rape victim — rape survivor | computer illiterate — technologically challenged
Best-answer traps
chairwoman, postwoman — still gendered, not neutral | his or her — fine, but the slides prefer their | informal settlers vs outdoor urban — no land title vs no home
Segmentals vs suprasegmentals
Segmentals — consonants, vowels, diphthongs | Suprasegmentals (prosodic features) — stress, pitch, intonation, length, tone, juncture
Spelling vs sound

to, too, two — different letters, same sound | cake, mat, call, any, sofa — same letter a, 5 sounds | rough, physics, head — 2 letters, 1 sound | bomb, knee, debt, receipt — silent letters | ghoti — fish (rough, women, nation)
Letter c
c + i, e, y — /s/ (city, cent, cyst) | c + a, o, u or word-final — /k/ (cat, cup, plastic) | p + h — /f/ (philosophy)
Places
Bilabial — p b m w | Labiodental — f v | Interdental — θ ð | Alveolar — t d s z n l r | Palatal — š ž č ǰ y | Velar — k g ŋ | Glottal — h ʔ
Manners
Stops/plosives — p b t d k g | Fricatives — f v θ ð s z š ž (h) | Affricates — č ǰ | Nasals — m n ŋ | Liquids — l (lateral), r (retroflex) | Glides — w y
Groups
Sibilants — hissing s z š ž | Obstruents — stops, fricatives, affricates | Voiceless (red) — p t k f θ s š h č | Voiced (black) — b d g v ð z ž ǰ m n ŋ l r w y
Odd one out
Same row — same manner | Same column — same place | Same color — same voicing | Bilabial + labiodental together — both use the lips
